extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and the moral/social sciences
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on proper method and common logical errors for constructing and evaluating arguments and theories in the moral and social sciences, including how to generalize methods from simpler sciences and how to understand causation and necessity for human actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: No a priori construction of principles of evidence or method
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles of Evidence and Theories of Method are not to be constructed à priori. The laws of our rational faculty, like those of every other natural agency, are only learnt by seeing the agent at work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier achievements of science were made without conscious observance of any Scientific Method; we learn how to ascertain truth by previously ascertaining many truths. Methods should be induced from successful practice, not dictated beforehand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn methods from simpler cases and generalize
rubrics_metrics.description: The way of obtaining the end is seen as it were instinctively by superior minds in some comparatively simple case, and is then, by judicious generalization, adapted to the variety of complex cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We learn to do a thing in difficult circumstances by attending to the manner in which we have spontaneously done the same thing in easier ones. Use exemplars from simpler sciences to form methods for more complex inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply stricter rules of induction in human/psychological inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Although several other sciences have emerged from a state of vague popular discussion, none now remain in it except those which relate to man himself...there is still much uncertainty and much controversy, which can only be terminated by the general acknowledgment and employment of stricter rules of induction than are commonly recognised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical knowledge of man has advanced; laws of Mind and Society remain disputed. To improve moral and social sciences, adopt and adapt the methods that have succeeded in the natural sciences, with attention to difficulties peculiar to human subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and adapt methods suited to particular branches of moral inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: It remains ... to examine which of those methods are more especially suited to the various branches of moral inquiry; under what peculiar facilities or difficulties they are there employed; how far the unsatisfactory state of those inquiries is owing to a wrong choice of methods, how far to want of skill in the application of right ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether poor results stem from misapplied methods or from inherent limits; select and adapt logical processes appropriate to each subfield rather than applying a one-size-fits-all method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test whether laws of causation apply to human actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the actions of human beings, like all other natural events, subject to invariable laws? Does that constancy of causation, which is the foundation of every scientific theory of successive phenomena, really obtain among them?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before treating human conduct as scientific, deliberately answer whether human actions exhibit the constancy of causation required for scientific law; this question is central to applying scientific methods to moral sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define Philosophical Necessity as predictability from motives and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Correctly conceived, the doctrine called Philosophical Necessity is simply this: that, given the motives which are present to an individual's mind, and given likewise the character and disposition of the individual, the manner in which he will act might be unerringly inferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical Necessity should be interpreted as uniformity of sequence and predictability given complete knowledge of antecedents, not as mystical irresistibleness; this interpretation aligns with universal experience and does not conflict with subjective feelings of freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misleading terminology (necessity ≠ irresistibleness)
rubrics_metrics.description: That word, in its other acceptations, involves much more than mere uniformity of sequence: it implies irresistibleness. Applied to the will, it only means that the given cause will be followed by the effect, subject to all possibilities of counteraction by other causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious using ordinary words (like 'necessity') that carry extra connotations; clarify terms to prevent the imagination from attributing a stronger bond (irresistibleness) than the intended regularity or predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat causes as controllable and recognize countervailing influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Human actions are never (except in some cases of mania) ruled by any one motive with such absolute sway, that there is no room for the influence of any other. The causes, therefore, on which action depends, are never uncontrollable; and any given effect is only necessary provided that the causes tending to produce it are not controlled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing necessity or causation in human behavior, account for multiple interacting causes and possibilities of counteraction; avoid claiming absolute determinism where causes can be influenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Petitio Principii (begging the question)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begging the question occurs when a premise is manifestly the same in sense with the conclusion, or is actually proved from it, or is such as the persons addressed are not likely to know or admit except as an inference from the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume the disputed point in the premises. Watch for disguised instances (e.g., asserting justice and wisdom 'must be something' in a sense that smuggles in the conclusion) and for premises that merely restate the conclusion in different words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid equivocation / ambiguous middle term
rubrics_metrics.description: A fallacy arises when a term in the premises has different meanings in different places (e.g., 'something' meaning substance in one premise and merely an object of thought in another), leading to an illicit inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure terms retain consistent senses across premises and conclusion; identify instances where verbal ambiguity conceals circular or invalid reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Ignoratio Elenchi (irrelevant conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignoratio Elenchi (irrelevant conclusion) consists in mistaking the conclusion which is to be proved, substituting various propositions for the one required, or proving something that answers a different purpose rather than the proposition in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute the particular for the universal or vice versa, or prove an emotionally effective but logically irrelevant point (e.g., make the audience laugh) to secure assent. Ensure the proposition established is the very one in dispute, not merely something that produces the same practical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on appeals to emotion or associative odium instead of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The sophist may excite emotion or employ the odiousness of a term (e.g., calling someone a 'rogue') to destroy the force of a defence, thereby securing practical assent without proving the disputed proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate arguments on their logical relevance and evidentiary support; identify tactics that substitute passion, ridicule, or associative disgust for substantive proof and discount them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match the proposition proved to the proposition required
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a fallacy to prove what was not denied or to disprove what was not asserted; to prove the atrocity of a fraud instead of proving that a prisoner committed the fraud, or to prove that a relief method is advantageous rather than that it is preferable to an alternative method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging an argument, verify that the exact proposition in dispute has been addressed; avoid accepting proofs that address a different question or only show something tangentially related.
